transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-09-10
Start: 15:00 PDT
Duration: ~72 minutes
Attendees: Samir (Redwood AE), Maya (Redwood SE), Owen (Redwood Platform), Lucas (Orion Infra), Hannah (Orion ML), Priya (Orion Security), Benji (Orion Product)

Summary: quick lab-style deep dive to reconcile multi-model routing costs (Llama/Mistral/Qwen + small MoE experiments) with KV cache pre-warm strategies and VPC/on-prem constraints. Customer wants a cost model and an experiment plan to keep tail latency < 250ms P95 for chat flows while staying within their monthly GPU budget.

Topics: runtime routing economics, rope scaling implications for long context, KV cache pre-warm vs on-demand, microbatch sizing, quantization tradeoffs for Qwen-style models, VPC private deploy checklist, basic security/KMS notes.

--- Transcript (timestamps approximate, transcription has a few artifacts) ---
[00:00] Samir: All right, thanks everyone for joining. umm today we'd like to run through two things, cost modeling for multi-model routing and then a short lab on KV pre-warm strategies — especially for long context chat where rope scaling hits you. Maya, you wanna kick off?
[00:18] Maya: Yeah, sure. hi folks. quick recap: Orion shared sample traffic and we saw a pretty bimodal request size — short prompts at 60 tokens and long conversations pushing 6k. our goal is to keep P95 latency under 250ms for short and under 1.2s for long, while keeping monthly GPU spend under $X (tbd).
[00:35] Lucas: yeah, that's right. and to be clear, our main worry is the tails when the model routes to the heavier Qwen or a full Llama-variant, and also the cost delta when MoE routes to many experts — that exploded our estimates last quarter.
[00:50] Maya: exactly. so first, routing cost model: we break requests into buckets by model preference, routing policy (latency-first, cost-first), and fallback policies. So if you do latency-first, we try small Llama or Mistral for short, and only route to Qwen for the heaviest queries. cost-first switches that.
[01:10] Hannah: can you give a concrete example? like, if a request hits Mistral and then does a rerank or an external tool call, how do you count tokens vs routing?
[01:23] Maya: good question. token accounting is per model invocation; so if you proxy through Mistral then call a tool that triggers Qwen, you pay both. our routing engine can do soft fallbacks: we can attempt Mistral and if quality thresholds fail, then transparently escalate to Qwen — but you pay for both in that case unless you use local reranks.
[01:45] Benji: we saw that in the POC — trying to fallback doubled our per-turn costs. is there a good way to avoid paying twice while keeping quality?
[01:56] Owen: yeah, we recommend hybrid reranking — do embedding-based lightweight rerank then only escalate when rerank confidence is low; that reduces full model calls. also aggressive prefix/KV caching helps for multi-turn.
[02:12] Lucas: on KV caching, our current implementation flushes session caches after 30 minutes inactivity; we see cold starts where the KV miss causes long latencies. can Redwood support pre-warming?
[02:26] Maya: absolutely. we have two approaches: active pre-warm (replay synthetic requests to populate KV stores) and passive warm (keep a tiny heartbeat traffic to keep caches hot). pre-warm can be scheduled before known peaks.
[02:38] Priya: security question: if we replay sample traffic for pre-warm, does that touch PII? we need to ensure redaction and KMS controls.
[02:48] Maya: yes — we recommend sanitized synthetic traces. Redwood Private with customer KMS lets you manage keys; our runbook has patterns for rolling redaction. we'll share the checklist.
[03:00] Hannah: about rope scaling: when we scale rope exponent or decay for longer contexts, we noticed generation quality improves but latencies jump and KV hit-rates drop; what's the tradeoff there?
[03:14] Maya: rope scaling changes positional embeddings — longer rope tends to blow up computation because attention windows and KV sizes grow. for runtime you can do two things: a) limit active KV window and rely on sticky cache for recent tokens b) use select quantization profiles that speed up attention kernels at cost of minor quality.
[03:33] Lucas: do you have benchmarks for Llama vs Mistral vs Qwen with rope at 8k contexts?
[03:40] Maya: we ran internal microbenchmarks. quick numbers: at 8k context, Mistral quantized to 4-bit gives ~1.9x speed vs full FP16 Llama on the same GPU for decode steps, but Qwen tends to be heavier per-token. however MoE variants blow up depending on active expert counts — cost can be 2.5x to 6x depending on sparsity and routing.
[04:05] Lucas: that matches our alarms. the MoE routing cost was the surprise — even with 2 experts active we saw big jumps.
[04:14] Maya: right — two key knobs: expert budget (max experts per token) and token affinity rules. reducing max experts to 1-2 keeps cost down but may affect quality. also you can do token-level affinity so only a subset of tokens route to MoE.
[04:30] Benji: thinking product-wise, we might prioritize quality on critical flows and use cost-first routing for chat summaries. how flexible is the routing policy to per-route configs?
[04:41] Samir: very flexible — per-route policy via the Console; you can pin a route to latency-first, cost-first, or even custom policies that use heuristics (user tier, token count, signal from client).
[04:55] Hannah: let's jump into the lab on KV pre-warm? we prepared a small harness. Lucas, you said you had sample traces — did you upload them?
[05:05] Lucas: yes, uploaded a 10k-row sample to the shared spreadsheet and put a link in the chat.
[05:12] Maya: perfect. we'll run two tests: 1) passive heartbeat (1 req / sec per session) for an hour, 2) active pre-warm replay of the 10k traces right before a simulated traffic burst. we'll compare P95 and cold-start counts.
[05:27] [background noise: typing]
[05:30] Samir: heads-up — this will involve spinning a small dedicated pool for the lab; we can estimate cost but it's minimal for the short run.
[05:38] [10:02] [note: jump in timestamps as some sections summarized]
[10:02] Maya: test 1 results (passive heartbeat): P95 for short requests dropped from 320ms cold to 210ms after hour of heartbeat, but long requests still hit 1.1s for some tail cases. cold-starts were reduced by ~72%.
[10:25] Hannah: interesting — passive heat lowered the short-tail a lot. what about active pre-warm?
[10:31] Maya: test 2 (active replay): immediate P95 drop to 190ms for short, long at 0.95s, cold-starts < 10%. however pre-warm cost in GPU time was higher — equal to roughly 6 hours of baseline serving due to the replay volume.
[10:50] Lucas: so pre-warm works, but it's expensive. can we do targeted pre-warm only for hot sessions (top X% of users) rather than all?
[10:59] Maya: yes — we support session-scoped pre-warm and segment-based pre-warm. target the sessions that exceed a conversation-length threshold and keep the rest passive. that gives much of the benefit at a fraction of cost.
[11:12] Priya: for private deployments, is pre-warm compatible with their KMS? we need to make sure keys are never exported to Redwood-hosted logs.
[11:20] Owen: in Private, logs are local and KMS keys are customer-managed; pre-warm replays run in-customer infra. Redwood's agent only coordinates, but data never leaves the VPC unless you explicitly allow it. will document this in the runbook.
[11:34] Samir: quick aside on microbatching: increasing microbatch size reduces per-token cost but increases tail for low-concurrency bursts. Hannah, your traffic is bursty, yes?
[11:45] Hannah: very bursty — we see spikes from user sessions starting concurrently.
[11:49] Maya: recommended approach: we do dynamic microbatch sizing — low latency traffic goes through a low-latency queue (small microbatch), background work uses larger microbatches. Console supports per-route batch caps and dynamic timers.
[12:03] Benji: what's the effect of quantization for Qwen? we tried 8-bit and saw quality drop on legal-text tasks.
[12:13] Maya: quant profiles matter. for Qwen-style models we recommend mixed quantization: keep key attention matmuls at higher precision and quantize FF layers more aggressively. Redwood Optimize has suggested profiles per model and workload; we can run a quick eval across your prompt set.
[12:30] Lucas: any gotchas with memory fragmentation when we use 4-bit? we previously saw OOM noise.
[12:36] Owen: memory fragmentation is real — fragmentation and kernel constraint can cause higher latency jitter. mitigation: pin model instances, warm memory with a dummy batch, and prefer fused kernels that compact memory layout. we'll share kernel config suggestions.
[12:52] [22:00] [summarized section: tradeoff table review]
[22:00] Maya: quick tradeoff table:
- Latency-first: high cost, lower tail latencies.
- Cost-first: lower spend, higher tail probability.
- Hybrid: use micro policies and per-route pins.
- Pre-warm: big tail reduction, upfront GPU burn.
- Targeted pre-warm: sweet spot for cost vs tail.

[22:30] Hannah: are there real examples of customers running MoE in production with cost controls?
[22:36] Maya: yes, a telco partner uses token-affinity + expert budget to cap cost — they route only intent-rich tokens to MoE and keep others on a smaller dense model. quality was acceptable for their use-case.
[22:48] Lucas: ok that seems promising. on the VPC/on-prem checklist — what's the minimal footprint to run just the inference plane?
[22:57] Owen: minimal on-prem: 2 boxes per model-shard for redundancy, a control-plane agent VM, and shared NFS or local SSD for KV. if you want higher throughput, add more GPU nodes. the checklist includes networking rules, ports, and KMS endpoints.
[23:14] Priya: SAML + SCIM works? audit logs?
[23:18] Owen: yes: SAML SSO via your IDP, SCIM for provisioning, audit logs captured locally and optionally shipped to your SIEM. we'll include log rotation and retention guidance.
[23:31] Benji: can we get a sample cost model that shows the break-even point for running MoE vs dense models for our traffic profile?
[23:39] Maya: yes — Samir will run a cost calc: inputs are traffic distribution, probability of routing to MoE, average tokens, and target tail. we'll provide a sensitivity sheet so you can tweak routing policies and see cost impact.
[23:52] Lucas: perfect. also for the KV pre-warm, can we run a short A/B where 10% of prod traffic is routed to pre-warmed instances and 90% normal, to validate in production?
[24:03] Samir: that's doable — use canary routing in Console: set 10% traffic to the pre-warmed pool for 24 hours, monitor P95 and cost delta. we recommend a rollback policy if tail rises.
[24:15] [noise: someone drops connection briefly]
[24:30] Maya: little note on telemetry: make sure your per-token traces include model version, expert_count (for MoE), and KV hit flags; those are essential to diagnosing tail events.
[24:45] Hannah: we'll add those fields to our traces.
[24:49] Benji: one final question on rope: is there an automated rope scaling suggestion in Redwood Optimize or do we tune manually?
[24:58] Maya: Redwood Optimize has heuristics: given your token-length distribution it suggests rope decay and whether to truncate or compress old tokens to KV. but for complex tasks we recommend a small sweep — we'll help run that.
[25:12] Samir: okay let's recap next steps and action items.
[25:18] Maya: action items (recap): Samir to share benchmark spreadsheet and cost calc; Maya will share VPC runbook and kernel config suggestions; Lucas to upload traffic traces and pick pilot window; Priya to share compliance constraints re: KMS and PII; Hannah to provide prompt set for quant eval.
[25:35] Lucas: I'll aim to provide traces by 9/12, and pick a pilot window for 9/20-9/21.
[25:42] Priya: I'll confirm KMS policy by 9/16.
[25:46] Samir: we'll schedule a follow-up to review the sensitivity sheet and the A/B plan in ~two weeks.
[25:52] Benji: great, thanks everyone.
